title: Did Vikings wear horned helmets?
hook: The most famous Viking helmet has no horns at all. Blame an opera.
summary: There’s no evidence they did: no horned Viking helmet has been found; the image came from 19th-century art and opera.
cardText: There’s no evidence they did. The best-known Viking helmet, found in Norway, has no horns. The image caught on in the 19th century, through paintings and the costumes for a Wagner opera.

cardBlocks.text: Picture a Viking and he’s probably wearing a horned helmet. Yet archaeologists have never found a Viking Age helmet like that. The best-known one, dug up at Gjermundbu in Norway in 1943, has a guard like a pair of spectacles to protect the face, and no horns.

Horned helmets did exist, but much earlier: the two from Viksø in Denmark date from the Bronze Age, around 900 BC, and were probably worn in religious ceremonies. The horned Viking took off in the 19th century, especially after costume designer Carl Emil Doepler put horns on the helmets for the 1876 premiere of Wagner’s opera The Ring of the Nibelung.
No horned Viking helmet has ever been found; the horns came from an 1876 opera and the art of the time.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The Gjermundbu helmet came from a very rich grave from the end of the 10th century. It was found by chance, when a farmer decided to remove a mound from his land in the middle of the Nazi occupation of Norway. For years it was called the world’s only Viking helmet; then a helmet found in the UK in the 1950s was also dated to the Viking Age, making it the second nearly complete one.

The two bronze Viksø helmets were found in 1942 in a bog on the Danish island of Zealand, where they had been left as offerings. Besides horns, they have eyes and beaks. Radiocarbon dating of organic material hidden inside one of the horns confirmed that they are about 2,000 years older than the Viking Age.

At around the same time, very similar images of horned warriors appear in Sardinia and southwest Spain. Bronze Age rock carvings in western Sweden and southern Norway also show human figures with horns on their heads.
From the opera stage to comics

Doepler wasn’t alone: in the 19th century, the Swedish painter Johan August Malmström also drew horned Vikings to illustrate the Norse sagas. These artists may have been inspired by ancient horned helmets being dug up at the time, later dated to well before the Vikings. After the opera, horns spread to plays, films, comics and children’s books. In images made during the Viking Age itself, warriors appear bareheaded or in simple helmets.

claims.text: No Viking Age helmet with horns has ever been found.

support.excerpt: “No, helmets from the Viking Age with horns on them have never been found,” Ingrid Ystgaard tells sciencenorway.no.
Mysteriously, Viking-Age helmets are almost as rare as hen’s teeth: one was found in Ringerike in Norway, looking rather like a Batman mask but without the pointy ears.
But, crucially, no horns.

support.excerpt: One originating source for the horned helmets has been pegged: they were used by Carl Emil Doepler, the costume designer for the premiere of Wagner’s opera Ring of the Nibelung at the Bayreuth Festival in 1876.

But in terms of enduring popularity we can probably blame Wagner, or at least his costume designer Carl Emil Doepler, who was responsible for the outfits of the first performance of the Ring cycle at the Bayreuth Festival in 1876 and decided to stick a few jaunty horns onto the helmets.
